reading.title: Three Appeals Behind Every Strong Speech
reading.purpose: Learn how skilled speakers blend trust, feeling, and logic to move an audience.
paras: More than two thousand years ago, Greek thinkers studied rhetoric, the art of using language to persuade an audience. They noticed that memorable speeches rarely depend on loud voices or clever tricks. Instead, strong speakers weave together three distinct appeals—trust, emotion, and reason—so their ideas land with both the mind and the heart.

The first appeal is ethos, the credibility a speaker earns through honesty, experience, and fair-mindedness. A pediatric nurse who speaks about neighborhood bike helmets carries instant authority, while a speaker who exaggerates statistics will quickly undermine that trust. Speakers also build trust when they invoke respected principles, calling on shared laws or community values that listeners already admire.

The second appeal is logos, an appeal to clear reason built on facts, measurements, and step-by-step logic. A cogent argument—one that is orderly, solid, and convincing—shows listeners exactly how the evidence supports the conclusion. Without logos, even the warmest speech can drift into empty promises. Good speakers also use a well-placed rhetorical question, asked for dramatic effect rather than a literal answer, to make listeners pause and weigh the proof.

The third appeal is pathos, an appeal to human feelings such as hope, pride, or compassion. A single true story about a rescued library or a neighbor who stepped in during a storm can resonate deeply, striking a chord that makes an idea feel personal and real. When a speaker is eloquent—fluent, graceful, and clear—all three appeals reinforce one another. Trust opens the door, logic builds the case, and feeling inspires people to act.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "cogent" most nearly means
choices: spoken loudly enough to fill a crowded school auditorium
clear, orderly, and convincing because of strong logic
filled with personal stories designed to make listeners cry
short enough to fit on a single poster or notebook card
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines cogent directly as "one that is orderly, solid, and convincing."

qs.q: Which sentence shows both how a speaker gains credibility and how a speaker can lose it?
choices: The first appeal is ethos, the credibility a speaker earns through honesty, experience, and fair-mindedness.
A pediatric nurse who speaks about neighborhood bike helmets carries instant authority, while a speaker who exaggerates statistics will quickly undermine that trust.
Speakers also build trust when they invoke respected principles, calling on shared laws or community values that listeners already admire.
Trust opens the door, logic builds the case, and feeling inspires people to act.
qs.why: This sentence contrasts a nurse's earned authority with exaggerating statistics, which weakens trust.

ev.text: A pediatric nurse who speaks about neighborhood bike helmets carries instant authority, while a speaker who exaggerates statistics will quickly undermine that trust.

qs.q: Why does a speaker ask a rhetorical question during a speech?
choices: To make listeners stop and think about the point rather than call out an answer.
To test whether the audience remembers facts from two thousand years ago.
To replace all statistics and evidence with a dramatic personal story.
To ask the crowd to vote on which shared law should be mentioned next.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that a rhetorical question is "asked for dramatic effect rather than a literal answer, to make listeners pause and weigh the proof."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Ancient Greek speeches were far more moving than modern community talks.
Emotional stories are always more persuasive than facts or expert credibility.
Effective persuasion combines credibility, solid reasoning, and genuine emotional connection.
Speakers should avoid asking questions because listeners prefer simple lists of data.
qs.why: The reading explains ethos, logos, and pathos and concludes that all three work together to open minds and inspire action.
